content:
{'translated': 'Earlier this month, Google released the all-new Pixel 11 series. Compared with the previous-generation Pixel 10 series, the phone itself has little difference, but it brings several welcome experience optimizations. One of them is a set of new camera processing options, allowing you to have more freedom to control the final look of your photos.'}

{'translated': 'With the iPhone 18 Pro launch just around the corner, I hope Apple can also introduce a similar feature.'}

{'translated': 'Pixel 11 adds a new camera feature called "Camera Looks", similar to "Photographic Styles" on iPhone, allowing you to adjust how the camera renders images before you take the shot. These adjustments are made before capture, so they are not simply filter effects.'}

{'translated': "Google offers multiple preset style options, similar to Apple's approach, and you can even fine-tune the details of each preset individually. In addition, there are several brand-new styles that cater to current trends in mobile photography: Editorial, Velvet, Classic, Digi, Black Tie and Minimal."}

{'translated': 'These styles deliberately move away from the highly polished look of smartphone photos, trying to recapture the flavor of old-fashioned photography. Digi, as the name suggests, reproduces the low dynamic range, high contrast and grainy feel of those compact point-and-shoot cameras from the 2010s.'}

{'translated': 'As for Minimal, it focuses on an extremely low-processing imaging style — most HDR computation is disabled, allowing the image to present the most raw recording from the smartphone sensor. You can head over to 9to5Google to check out the related sample photos.'}

{'translated': 'On iPhone, with ProRAW you can theoretically restore photos to a nearly unprocessed state, but doing so defeats the purpose of shooting with a phone.'}

{'translated': 'Summary'}

{'translated': 'If Apple wants to build the best camera that fits in your pocket, it must face up to the fact that not every user is after the same look. Photographic Styles is a good first step, but Apple should go further. After all, photography is an art of self-expression, and giving users more control over the degree of photo processing would be a great improvement. Apple should take a page out of Google\'s book and add a "Minimal" style to iPhone.'}

{'translated': "What do you think of iPhone's current photographic performance? Do you like Apple's latest generation of Photographic Styles? Or do you feel there are still shortcomings? Feel free to let us know in the comments section."}
